name: Aleniglipron

lead: Aleniglipron is an experimental once-daily oral GLP-1 agonist for obesity. It is a small-molecule pill rather than an injectable peptide, so fat-loss followers watch it as a non-injectable option for lower appetite, weight loss and a leaner body.

It activates the GLP-1 receptor, the pathway used by semaglutide and similar drugs that reduces appetite and food intake. In the 36-week ACCESS phase 2b trial of 230 adults, placebo-adjusted weight loss was 8.2%, 9.8% and 11.3% across three dose arms. Phase 3 trials (ACCOMPLISH-1 and -2) began in 2026.

paras: It is available only in clinical trials, taken as a once-daily pill. Weight change built over the 36 weeks of the phase 2b trial.

Gastrointestinal events were the main adverse effects and were mostly mild to moderate; 10.4% of drug-arm participants stopped treatment for treatment-related reasons, and no drug-induced liver injury was reported. It is not approved and long-term data are lacking.

angle.text: Aleniglipron is an experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill: it lowers appetite for weight loss and a leaner body without injections. Phase 2b showed about 8-11% placebo-adjusted weight loss over 36 weeks; phase 3 is under way.

lead: Aleniglipron (development code GSBR-1290) is an investigational once-daily oral, small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist being developed by Structure Therapeutics for obesity and overweight.[1][2] Unlike injectable peptide GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide, it is a non-peptide pill, so it activates the same receptor without being a peptide.[3][2] It is of interest to people who want to lose body fat, and with it the changes in waist, face and overall shape that follow, without injections.

In the ACCESS phase 2b trial, 230 adults with obesity or overweight received aleniglipron or placebo for 36 weeks. Placebo-adjusted weight change was -8.2%, -9.8% and -11.3% at the 45, 90 and 120 mg arms, respectively. Gastrointestinal events were generally mild to moderate, treatment-related discontinuations were 10.4% across drug arms, and no drug-induced liver injury was reported.[1]
The drug is not approved anywhere. Phase 3 trials (ACCOMPLISH-1 and ACCOMPLISH-2) began recruiting in July 2026.[4][5]

paras: Aleniglipron is being developed for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight and at least one weight-related condition, and separately for people with type 2 diabetes.[4][5][6][7] Loss of body fat after reduced food intake is what changes visible shape, which is why obesity drugs attract interest in appearance-focused communities. The drug is available only to trial participants.

Aleniglipron activates the GLP-1 receptor, the same target as injectable agents used for weight management. Small-molecule agonists are a distinct chemical class from peptides; a structural review notes four known chemotypes of small-molecule GLP-1R agonists, which offer potential advantages in accessibility and patient convenience compared with peptide agonists.[8] A scoping review of small-molecule GLP-1 agonists describes oral availability as a way around the adherence and combination-therapy limits of subcutaneous injection.[9]
Wikipedia gives aleniglipron the formula C49H55FN9O6P and a molar mass of about 916 g/mol, with a phosphine oxide group and several fused heterocyclic rings including an oxadiazolone.[2]

Structure Therapeutics discovered and developed the compound; a June 2023 abstract in the journal Diabetes described its discovery, and a phase 2a study in type 2 diabetes and obesity began in May 2023.[2] In June 2024 the company reported positive topline phase 2a obesity data with statistically significant placebo-adjusted weight loss and favourable tolerability.[2] The phase 2b ACCESS trial began in October 2024, and its results were published in Nature Medicine in 2026.[1][6]

The ACCESS trial (NCT06693843) was randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled. Participants (mean BMI 39.5, 54 percent female) received once-daily aleniglipron, escalated every 4 weeks to 45, 90 or 120 mg. At week 36 all doses significantly outperformed placebo on the primary endpoint, with no apparent weight-loss plateau, and an interim look at the open-label extension showed continued weight loss. Vomiting rarely recurred after reintroduction following permitted dose interruptions.[1][6] A publisher correction to the paper has been issued.[10]

Additional phase 2 studies in people with type 2 diabetes (n=58), a body-composition study (n=71) and a dose-range study (n=85) are registered as completed.[7][11][12] A pooled analysis of randomised trials of oral non-peptide GLP-1 agonists in people without diabetes, posted as a preprint, examines the class as a whole.[3]
ACCOMPLISH-1 (3,600 participants with obesity or overweight and a weight-related condition, started July 2026) and ACCOMPLISH-2 (1,100 participants with type 2 diabetes) are recruiting.[4][5]

In ACCESS the reported tolerability profile was consistent with the GLP-1 receptor agonist class: gastrointestinal events were typically mild to moderate and became less frequent over time. Treatment-related discontinuations were 10.4 percent across drug arms and no drug-induced liver injury was reported.[1] A dedicated hepatic impairment pharmacokinetic study is registered but not yet recruiting.[13]

Aleniglipron is an unapproved investigational drug with no marketing authorisation, price or coverage. It belongs to a wave of oral GLP-1 candidates developed as needle-free alternatives to injectable weight-loss drugs.[3][3]

timeline.event: Phase 2a study begins (May); discovery abstract presented (June).[2]
Topline phase 2a obesity data (June); phase 2b ACCESS begins (October).[6][2]
ACCESS results published in Nature Medicine; phase 3 ACCOMPLISH trials start.[1][4][5]
